query: Eutectic high-entropy alloys contain dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking can initiate and lead to catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation. Conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility, while the wide range of previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility? State one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

revised_generation.hypothesis: Intervention of eutectic high-entropy alloys (EHEAs) can improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility.
revised_generation.material_initial_state: Eutectic high-entropy alloys (EHEAs) with dual-phase lamellar colonies and numerous internal boundaries.
revised_generation.intervention: Alloy design strategy using the concept of EHEAs.
revised_generation.mechanism: The EHEA concept combines the advantages of both HEAs and eutectic alloys.
revised_generation.predicted_outcome: Improved strength and room-temperature tensile ductility, with a yield strength of at least 1000 MPa and an elongation at break of at least 10%.
revised_generation.boundary: Industrial scale, defined as a production volume of at least 100 kg, and low cost, defined as a cost per kilogram of less than $100.
revised_generation.uncertainty: Further exploration of new EHEAs is needed, particularly in terms of optimizing the composition and processing conditions to achieve reliable and reproducible results.
revised_generation.falsification_experiment: Testing the alloy design strategy using the concept of EHEAs on a larger scale, with a sample size of at least 10 specimens, using a conventional casting method, and evaluating the strength and ductility using standardized tensile testing methods. The experiment will be considered falsified if the resulting alloys do not exhibit a yield strength of at least 1000 MPa and an elongation at break of at least 10%.

cited_evidence.text: As such, our alloy design strategy resulted in the discovery of an EHEA with a fine lamellar fcc/B2 structure and balanced high fracture strength and high ductility. This novel strategy is promising to solve the problems inhibiting the engineering application of HEAs as high-temperature materials, including the inferior castability and compositional segregation, and the conflict between high fracture strength and high ductility. In addition, this novel strategy also brought breakthrough to NiAl-based alloys in significantly enhancing the ductility at room temperature while simultaneously achieving the high strength. The EHEA concept, combining the advantages of both HEAs and eutectic alloys, and at the same time eliminating the disadvantages of these two types of alloys, leads to a promising new class of high-temperature alloys. Using this new alloy design strategy, an industrial scale HEA with uniform organizations and compositions can be prepared by the conventional casting method in a low cost way, allowing for large-scale industrial applications.
